cmo-cmo-2017-01.title: Shift the smallest variable to 0
cmo-cmo-2017-01.body:
The expression is symmetric in $a, b, c$, so we may assume $a > b > c \ge 0$. Put $a' = a - c$, $b' = b - c$; then $a' > b' > 0$, $0 \le a' \le a$ and $0 \le b' \le b$. The denominators depend only on differences, which do not change, while the numerators do not increase:
$$\frac{a^2}{(b - c)^2} + \frac{b^2}{(c - a)^2} + \frac{c^2}{(a - b)^2} \ \ge\ \frac{a'^2}{b'^2} + \frac{b'^2}{a'^2} + 0 .$$
With $x = \frac{a'^2}{b'^2} > 0$ we have $x + \frac1x - 2 = \frac{(x - 1)^2}{x} > 0$, because $x \ne 1$ (as $a' \ne b'$). Hence the left side is $> 2$. ∎

cmo-cmo-2017-01.title: A perfect-square identity
cmo-cmo-2017-01.body:
For distinct $a, b, c$ one can verify (expand, or check with a computer algebra system) the identity
$$\frac{a^2}{(b - c)^2} + \frac{b^2}{(c - a)^2} + \frac{c^2}{(a - b)^2} - 2 = \left(\frac{a(a - b)(a - c) + b(b - a)(b - c) + c(c - a)(c - b)}{(a - b)(b - c)(c - a)}\right)^2 .$$
So the left side is at least $2$, with equality only if the Schur expression $N = a(a - b)(a - c) + b(b - a)(b - c) + c(c - a)(c - b)$ vanishes. By Schur's inequality (for non-negative reals), $N \ge 0$ with equality only when $a = b = c$ or when two of the numbers are equal and the third is $0$. Neither can happen for three distinct numbers, so $N > 0$ and the left side is $> 2$. ∎

(Schur's inequality with its equality case: for $a \ge b \ge c \ge 0$, $N = (a - b)\big[a(a - c) - b(b - c)\big] + c(a - c)(b - c)$; both terms are $\ge 0$ since $a(a-c) \ge b(b-c)$, and for distinct $a > b > c$ the first term is positive.)

cmo-cmo-2017-02.title: Commute f with the divisor function
cmo-cmo-2017-02.body:
Let $d(n)$ be the number of divisors of $n$, so $d(n) = f(f(n))$ and
$$f(d(n)) = f(f(f(n))) = d(f(n)) \qquad\text{for all } n. \tag{$*$}$$
Facts about $d$: $d(1) = 1$, $d(2) = 2$, $d(n) \ge 2$ for $n \ge 2$, and $d(n) < n$ for $n > 2$ (the divisors are among $1, \ldots, n$ but $n - 1$ is not one of them, as $n - 1 \nmid n$ for $n > 2$). Also $d(n) = 1$ only for $n = 1$, and $d(n) = 2$ exactly when $n$ is prime.

**Claim: $f(2) = 2$.** Let $m = f(2)$; then $f(m) = f(f(2)) = d(2) = 2$.

- *If $m \ge 2$:* let $m_0$ be the smallest integer $\ge 2$ with $f(m_0) = 2$. By $(*)$, $f(d(m_0)) = d(f(m_0)) = d(2) = 2$, and $d(m_0) \ge 2$, so by minimality $d(m_0) \ge m_0$. As $d(n) < n$ for $n > 2$, this forces $m_0 = 2$, i.e. $f(2) = 2$.
- *If $m = 1$:* then $f(1) = f(f(2)) = 2$. For every prime $p$, $(*)$ gives $d(f(p)) = f(d(p)) = f(2) = 1$, so $f(p) = 1$. Then for a prime $p$, $d(f(p^2)) = f(d(p^2)) = f(3) = 1$ (as $3$ is prime), so $f(p^2) = 1$ and $3 = d(p^2) = f(f(p^2)) = f(1) = 2$ — a contradiction.

So $f(2) = 2$.

**Conclusion.** For a prime $p$, by $(*)$, $d(f(p)) = f(d(p)) = f(2) = 2$, so $f(p)$ has exactly two divisors: it is prime. ∎

(Such functions do exist; one can be constructed inductively.)

cmo-cmo-2017-03.title: Reflect the set
cmo-cmo-2017-03.body:
For a nonempty $T \subseteq S_n$ let $A(T)$ be its average and $M(T)$ its median, and let $T^* = \{n + 1 - t : t \in T\}$. The map $x \mapsto n + 1 - x$ reverses order, so $M(T^*) = n + 1 - M(T)$, and clearly $A(T^*) = n + 1 - A(T)$. Hence
$$M(T) > A(T) \iff M(T^*) < A(T^*).$$
So $T \mapsto T^*$ is a bijection (it is its own inverse) between the sets with $M > A$ and the sets with $M < A$; let each of these classes have $B$ elements. Every nonempty subset is in exactly one of the classes $M > A$, $M < A$, $M = A$, so the number of balanced subsets is
$$(2^n - 1) - 2B,$$
which is odd. ∎

cmo-cmo-2017-03.title: Count the symmetric sets
cmo-cmo-2017-03.body: Pair each balanced $T$ with $T^*$ (also balanced, by the formulas above). Pairs with $T \ne T^*$ contribute an even number, so it suffices to count balanced $T$ with $T = T^*$. A symmetric $T$ is automatically balanced: its elements pair up as $t, n + 1 - t$, so $A(T) = M(T) = \frac{n+1}{2}$. A symmetric $T$ is determined by $U = T \cap \{1, \ldots, \lceil n/2\rceil\}$, which is nonempty (for $t \in T$, $\min(t, n + 1 - t) \le \frac{n+1}{2}$, so it is $\le \lceil n/2 \rceil$), and every nonempty $U$ arises (from $T = U \cup \{n + 1 - u : u \in U\}$). So there are $2^{\lceil n/2 \rceil} - 1$ symmetric sets — an odd number. Hence the total is odd. ∎

cmo-cmo-2017-04.title: Complex numbers
cmo-cmo-2017-04.body:
Place $B$ at the origin, $A = a$, $C = c$ (complex numbers), so $D = a + c$. Orient the plane so that $0 < \arg(c/a) < \pi$, and let $\omega = e^{i\pi/3}$, so $\omega^2 = \omega - 1$ and $\bar\omega^2 = \bar\omega - 1$.

**Locating $P$ and $Q$.** $P$ is the apex of an equilateral triangle on $BA$, so $P = a\omega$ or $P = a\bar\omega$. Since $P$ is inside the parallelogram, it lies on the same side of line $BA$ as $C$, i.e. $0 < \arg(P/a) < \pi$: so $P = a\omega$. Similarly $Q$ is on the same side of line $BC$ as $A$, i.e. $-\pi < \arg(Q/c) < 0$, so $Q = c\bar\omega$.

**$DPQ$ is equilateral.**
$$P - D = a(\omega - 1) - c = a\omega^2 - c, \qquad Q - D = c(\bar\omega - 1) - a = c\bar\omega^2 - a.$$
Then $\omega (P - D) = a\omega^3 - c\omega = -a - c\omega$, and $-\bar\omega^2 = \omega$ (since $\bar\omega^2 = e^{-2\pi i/3} = -\omega$), so $c\bar\omega^2 - a = -c\omega - a$. Hence $Q - D = \omega(P - D)$: triangle $DPQ$ is equilateral. It is non-degenerate, because $P = D$ would put $P$ at a vertex, not inside.

**The intersection point.** Let $O = \frac{D + P + Q}{3}$ be the centre of the equilateral triangle $DPQ$ and $K = 2O - D$ the point diametrically opposite $D$ on its circumcircle. By Thales, $\angle DPK = \angle DQK = 90^\circ$, so $K$ lies on both perpendiculars; as $D, P, Q$ are not collinear the two perpendiculars are not parallel, so $K$ is their intersection point. Now
$$K = \frac{2P + 2Q - D}{3} = \frac{a(2\omega - 1) + c(2\bar\omega - 1)}{3} = \frac{i\sqrt3\,a - i\sqrt3\,c}{3} = \frac{i}{\sqrt3}(a - c),$$
using $2\omega - 1 = i\sqrt3$ and $2\bar\omega - 1 = -i\sqrt3$. Thus $K - B = K$ is a real multiple of $i(a - c)$, i.e. perpendicular to $AC$. Hence $K$ lies on the line through $B$ perpendicular to $AC$ — the altitude from $B$ in triangle $ABC$. ∎

cmo-cmo-2017-04.title: Congruent triangles (official)
cmo-cmo-2017-04.body:
Let $m = \angle ABC$. Since $P, Q$ are inside, $\angle ABC > 60^\circ$ and $\angle DAB = 180^\circ - m > 60^\circ$, so $60^\circ < m < 120^\circ$. Then
$$\angle DAP = (180^\circ - m) - 60^\circ = 120^\circ - m,\quad \angle DCQ = (180^\circ - m) - 60^\circ = 120^\circ - m,\quad \angle PBQ = 60^\circ - (m - 60^\circ) = 120^\circ - m,$$
and $AD = BC = BQ = CQ$, $AP = AB = BP = CD$. So triangles $DAP$, $QBP$, $QCD$ are congruent (SAS) and $DP = PQ = QD$.

Let $O$ be the centre of the equilateral triangle $DPQ$. From the congruence $DAP \cong QCD$, $\angle PDA = \angle DQC$, hence $\angle ODA = \angle PDA + 30^\circ = \angle DQC + 30^\circ = \angle OQC$; with $OD = OQ$ and $DA = QC$, triangles $ODA$ and $OQC$ are congruent and $OA = OC$. So $O$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $AC$, which passes through the midpoint $M$ of $AC$ — also the midpoint of $BD$.

The two perpendicular lines meet at the antipode $K$ of $D$ on the circle $DPQ$, so $O$ is the midpoint of $DK$. In triangle $DBK$, $OM$ joins the midpoints of $DK$ and $DB$, so $BK \parallel OM \perp AC$: $K$ lies on the altitude from $B$. ∎

cmo-cmo-2017-05.title: Project onto a well-chosen line
cmo-cmo-2017-05.body:
Let $S$ be the set of the $100$ centres. If all centres coincide, any line through that point meets all circles. Otherwise let $A, B \in S$ be a pair at the maximal distance $d > 0$, and let $\ell$ be a line perpendicular to $AB$.

**The projections of $S$ on $\ell$ lie in a short interval.** For any other centre $C$, the triangle $ABC$ has area $\frac12 d\cdot \operatorname{dist}(C, AB) \le 2017$, so $\operatorname{dist}(C, AB) \le \frac{4034}{d}$. Projecting onto $\ell$ measures exactly this signed distance from line $AB$, so all projections lie in an interval of length $\frac{8068}{d}$ around the point $\ell \cap AB$. On the other hand, the distance between two projections is at most the distance between the points, which is $\le d$. So the projections lie in an interval of length at most
$$\min\left(d, \frac{8068}{d}\right) \le \sqrt{8068} < 90 .$$

**Overlapping shadows.** A line perpendicular to $\ell$ through a point $x \in \ell$ meets a circle of radius $1$ exactly when $x$ lies in the projection of the circle, an interval of length $2$ centred at the projection of its centre. These $100$ intervals lie inside one interval $I$ of length $< 90 + 2 = 92$. Let $N(x)$ be the number of these intervals containing $x$. Then
$$\int_I N(x)\,dx = 100 \cdot 2 = 200 .$$
If $N(x) \le 2$ for every $x$, the integral would be at most $2\cdot 92 = 184 < 200$. Hence some $x$ lies in at least three of the intervals, and the line through $x$ perpendicular to $\ell$ intersects at least three of the circles. ∎
